summary: Specifies a mechanism that lets two parties using GSS-API choose which security mechanism they will both use. It makes negotiation of authentication possible without prior agreement. It was a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 4178.

eli5.summary: Two people who speak many languages first check which one they both know. SPNEGO lets two programs find a security method they both understand.

questions: what is the oid for spnego
subtitle: Letting two programs find a security method they both understand, without prior agreement.

tldr.problem: GSS-API provides a generic interface for security but doesn't tell two parties how to discover which security mechanism they both support.
tldr.mechanism: SPNEGO is a pseudo-security mechanism that runs a negotiation exchange where the initiator proposes one or more security mechanisms and the target selects one, all within the GSS-API protocol itself.
tldr.outcome: Two parties can establish a security context without needing to agree in advance on which security mechanism to use. SPNEGO was superseded by RFC 4178 in 2005.

today: RFC 2478 is obsoleted by RFC 4178, which improved the mechanism. However, the core concept remains in use: SPNEGO is still widely deployed in Kerberos environments for authentication negotiation.

sections.title: What SPNEGO Solves
sections.content:
GSS-API is a generic interface that lets applications use different security mechanisms underneath—Kerberos, NTLM, or others—as long as both sides support the same mechanism. But GSS-API itself does not define how two applications discover which mechanism they have in common.

SPNEGO (the Simple and Protected GSS-API Negotiation Mechanism) is a pseudo-security mechanism, identified by the OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.2. It wraps the GSS-API calls that the two sides make, intercepting the security context establishment and using it to run a negotiation exchange. Once both sides agree on a mechanism, the actual security work happens with that mechanism.
sections.eli5: Imagine two people meeting: one speaks English and Spanish, the other speaks English and French. Before they talk, they check which language they both know. SPNEGO does that for security mechanisms.

sections.title: How the Negotiation Works
sections.content:
The initiator (the side starting the connection) calls the standard GSS-API function to set up a security context, but using SPNEGO. This triggers the initiator to send a token containing a list of security mechanisms it supports, ordered by preference, along with optional flags describing what the mechanism should offer (mutual authentication, confidentiality, etc.).

The target (the receiving side) gets that token and looks at the list. If it supports the first mechanism on the list, it can respond immediately saying 'I accept your first choice' and optionally include the first response token from that mechanism. If it doesn't support the preferred mechanism but supports another one from the list, it says 'I accept this other one instead'. If it supports nothing on the list, it rejects the negotiation.

To avoid wasting a round trip, the initiator can include the initial security token for its preferred mechanism right in the first negotiation token. If the target also prefers that mechanism, both sides can complete setup in a single round trip instead of two.
sections.eli5: One person says 'I know Kerberos or NTLM, I prefer Kerberos.' The other says 'I only know Kerberos, let's use that' and can start the real security handshake right away.

sections.title: The Negotiation Tokens
sections.content:
All SPNEGO negotiation data travels inside two ASN.1 structures that the RFC calls NegTokenInit (sent by the initiator) and NegTokenTarg (sent by the target).

The NegTokenInit contains: the list of mechanism OIDs the initiator supports, a set of flags (delegation, mutual authentication, replay protection, etc.), an optional initial security token for the preferred mechanism, and an optional integrity check (mechListMIC) over the mechanism list.

The NegTokenTarg contains: the negotiation result (accepted, incomplete, or rejected), the selected mechanism (if accepted), the response to the initial token (if one was sent), and an optional integrity check. When the selected mechanism supports integrity protection, the target MUST include a mechListMIC—a message integrity code over the original mechanism list—so the initiator can verify the list wasn't tampered with.
sections.eli5: The negotiation messages are like envelopes: the first says 'here are my choices' and optionally 'here's the first handshake', the second says 'I pick this one' and optionally 'here's my answer'.

sections.title: Protecting the Negotiation
sections.content:
The negotiation exchange itself is vulnerable to attack: a network attacker could trick one side into using a weaker security mechanism than it would prefer. SPNEGO defends against this when the selected mechanism supports integrity protection.

If the mechanism selected by the target can compute message integrity codes (MICs), then before the final security token, the target computes a MIC over the original list of mechanisms from the initiator and sends it. The initiator verifies this MIC, ensuring that the list it sent has not been modified. If the MIC is missing or invalid, the context establishment fails.

For mechanisms that use an even number of message exchanges, the target sends the MIC in its final response. For mechanisms using an odd number of exchanges, there is a trade-off: either the initiator sends a final token with the MIC (saving a round trip but giving the target no proof the list was not modified) or the target sends an extra message containing only the MIC.
sections.eli5: Once the two sides agree on a method, they can ask the method to verify that their earlier choice was not changed in transit. If it was, they stop and start over.

sections.title: Negotiation Scenarios
sections.content:
When an initiator supporting Kerberos and NTLM sends a token to a target that only supports Kerberos, the negotiation is straightforward: the target accepts Kerberos, and both sides continue with the Kerberos context establishment.

When the initiator supports two mechanisms but the target supports only the second, the target rejects the preferred mechanism and proposes the second one. The initiator then switches to that mechanism for the remainder of the exchange.

If the initiator embeds the initial Kerberos token in the negotiation token (optimistic negotiation) and the target also prefers Kerberos, the target can immediately accept the preference, process the initial token, and send back its answer—all in the first round trip. This is a key optimization for performance on high-latency networks.
sections.eli5: One side sends a list; the other picks from it or rejects it all. If both picked the same favorite at the start, they can skip the negotiation steps and get straight to the real work.
